title: Nokia: From 40% of Phones to Selling the Business
description:
At the end of 2007, Nokia estimated it sold about 4 in every 10 phones in the world. The first iPhone shipped that same year. By mid-2013, Gartner put Nokia at 14% of phone sales, and Microsoft agreed to buy its phone business plus a patent licence for EUR 5.44 billion (about $7.2 billion). In 2015 Microsoft took a $7.6 billion impairment charge tied to the deal and cut up to 7,800 jobs (Microsoft's own accounts put the total purchase price at $9.5 billion, including $1.5 billion of cash acquired). Nokia itself survived as a network equipment company. The lesson: success can make you slow to change.

Sources: Nokia Q4 and full-year 2007 results, Form 6-K (Jan 24, 2008); Gartner mobile phone sales, Q2 2013 (Aug 14, 2013); Stephen Elop memo to Nokia staff (Feb 2011, published by Engadget, Feb 8, 2011); Microsoft press releases (Sept 3, 2013; July 8, 2015); Microsoft Form 10-K for fiscal 2014 (Note 9, filed July 31, 2014); TechCrunch (Sept 2, 2013) for the dollar conversion; Nokia release on completing the sale (Apr 25, 2014). Market share figures come from Nokia's own estimate (2007) and Gartner (2013), which use different methods.

scenes.say: By mid twenty thirteen, Gartner put Nokia at fourteen percent.
Microsoft paid about seven point two billion for the phone unit and patent rights.
Now the twist: the buyer got burned too.
Two years later, Microsoft wrote off seven point six billion dollars.
Nokia survived as a network equipment company.
The lesson: when you're winning, ask what could replace your best product.
Being on top guarantees nothing. Ask Nokia.
